evidence.claim: DeRidder’s former parish jail has Gothic Revival features more familiar from colleges and churches: shallow arches, dormer windows and a central tower.
evidence.quote: The structure has the characteristics of the collegiate Gothic Revival architectural style, with shallow arches, dormer windows, and a central tower. This style was popular with colleges, universities, and churches.

evidence.claim: Inside, a spiral staircase gave access to cells equipped with a toilet, shower, lavatory and window.
evidence.quote: there was a toilet, shower, lavatory, and window in each cell. A large spiral staircase gave access to each cell.

evidence.claim: A tunnel connected the jail with the courthouse for moving prisoners to trial.
evidence.quote: There is a tunnel leading from the courthouse to the jail that was used to transport prisoners for trial.

evidence.claim: Two men convicted of murdering taxi driver J. J. Brevelle were hanged here on March 9, 1928.
evidence.quote: The two men who were found guilty of his murder were hanged in the old parish jail on March 9, 1928.

evidence.claim: The executions gave the building its Hanging Jail name.
evidence.quote: It was after this incident, the Beauregard Parish Jail, sometimes referred to as the Gothic jail, also became known as the Hanging Jail

evidence.claim: The bottom floor contained quarters for the jailer as well as a kitchen.
evidence.quote: There was a jailers' quarters on the bottom floor as well as a kitchen.

flags: Partial route identity: cache documents Myths and Legends Byway, not the formal designation or renaming of Attakapas-Coushatta. Do not equate the catalog’s 23.2 mapped miles with the larger 181-mile byway.

Cache gives flat terrain and route connections but little road character or construction history. Ferry history supplies transport context; the overview stays shorter rather than inventing grades or drive time.
Atakapa in the tourism source differs from Attakapas in the catalog name. No tribal-authored cache page supports a fuller Indigenous history; omitted the current draft’s first-settled formulation.

Omitted the current claim that France, New Spain, Mexico and the United States all disputed the border after the Louisiana Purchase: sources compress different periods. Burr Ferry page has internally faulty chronology, including treaty ratification in 1921.

Jail sources disagree on 1914 versus 1915 and on present use. Archived tourism and courthouse pages offer tours; jail page says not in use. Current open-now claim omitted. No access promised to its blocked tunnel.
Leather Britches story is retained as the tourism office’s account, not independently verified labor history or a statement of current community sentiment.
Burr Ferry precedes the supplied strip; Merryville mile 4.07 and DeRidder mile 22.94 set the remaining moment order. Current story has no story-level motifs; output uses an empty list.
Merryville is kept below 90 words: the cached strike story lacks sufficient independent detail for a longer account.
